title: Work function and stopping voltage
log: 2026-11-01T14:46:41Z match: Claude Haiku 5.5 found no bank point the same, so it is written new
2026-11-02T04:35:43Z autoreview: cleared with the fix (b wording)

match.reason: The closest bank point, the photoelectric effect, covers threshold frequency and photons but never defines the work function or the stopping voltage, so the new point teaches a narrower idea that needs its own card.

draft.title: Work function and stopping voltage
card: Work function
the least energy needed to free an electron from a metal's surface. It is written as φ and depends on the metal.
Maximum kinetic energy
an electron freed with the least energy loss leaves with the most kinetic energy. This is Kmax = hf - φ.
Stopping voltage
the voltage that just stops the fastest electrons from reaching the other plate. Kmax = eV₀, where e is the charge of an electron.
Measuring V₀ gives Kmax in electron volts. If V₀ is 2.0 V, then Kmax is 2.0 eV.
draft.remember: Kmax = hf - φ, and the stopping voltage V₀ measures Kmax through Kmax = eV₀.

a.q: A metal has a work function of 2.0 eV. A photon of energy 5.0 eV frees an electron with the most kinetic energy possible. What stopping voltage is needed?
a.why: Kmax = 5.0 eV - 2.0 eV = 3.0 eV, so the stopping voltage is 3.0 V. A student who gives 5.0 V forgets that some of the photon's energy was used to free the electron.
a.clue: Take the work function away from the photon energy first.

b.q: Light of one frequency ejects electrons from metal X, which has a stopping voltage of 1.5 V. The same light is used on metal Y, which has a larger work function. What is the stopping voltage for Y?
opts: Zero, because no electrons are ejected
b.why: The photon energy is the same, so a larger work function leaves less energy for motion. Kmax is lower, so V₀ is lower. We cannot say that no electrons are ejected, because Y may still have a work function below the photon energy.
b.clue: Same photon energy: if more is spent freeing the electron, how much is left?

problems.detail: The question does not say whether Y's work function is still below the photon energy. If it is not, no electrons are ejected, so a careful student may hesitate over the 'Zero' option. 'Less than 1.5 V' still covers both cases, but adding 'electrons are still ejected from Y' would remove the doubt.

check.summary: The physics and both answers are correct. Question b would be clearer if it stated that Y still emits electrons, so the 'Zero' option is plainly wrong.
